extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing whether patent claims meet the subject-matter eligibility requirements of 35 U.S.C. §101 (i.e., whether claims fall within statutory categories and avoid judicial exceptions), including examples, allowed claim amendments, and proper examiner actions/rejections. Intended to direct examination practice and record-keeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory subject-matter categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The four statutory categories of invention: Process, Machine, Manufacture, or Composition of Matter and improvements thereof. Process = "an act, or series of acts or steps"; Machine = "a concrete thing, consisting of parts, or of certain devices and combination of devices"; Manufacture = "an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving these materials new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations"; Composition of Matter = "all compositions of two or more substances and all composite articles..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimed invention must fall within at least one of these categories to be eligible. Identification of a single category is not necessary; a claim may satisfy more than one. Analyze based on the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). See MPEP 2106(I) for definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to fall within a statutory category (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed inventions that do not fall within the statutory categories are not eligible for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If under the BRI a claim covers an invention that does not fall within one of the four statutory categories, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. §101 must be made. A claim that covers both eligible and ineligible subject matter should be rejected because the BRI covers ineligible subject matter. Use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., ¶¶ 7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts have interpreted the statutory categories to exclude 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas' (the 'judicial exceptions'). These terms cover the basic tools of scientific and technological work, such as scientific principles, naturally occurring phenomena, mental processes, and mathematical algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim falls within a statutory category, the examiner must still analyze whether it is directed to a judicial exception. For example, a process that meets the statutory definition could be ineligible if it is directed to an abstract idea and does not recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance: examination principles
rubrics_metrics.description: For examination of all claims the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance directs: use the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim; analyze the claim as a whole; practice compact prosecution by fully examining under 35 U.S.C. §§102, 103, 112 and 101; and take a comprehensive view of subject matter eligibility incorporating relevant case law (Alice, Myriad, Mayo, Bilski).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim falls within at least one statutory category, proceed to judicial exception analysis. Apply BRI and analyze the claim as a whole rather than dissecting in isolation. Consider the full body of case law in performing the eligibility determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory examples — intangible subject matter (business models, information collections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of claims that do not fall within the statutory categories: a 'paradigm for marketing software' (business model) and a 'device profile' (an intangible collection of information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These intangible items are not a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter and should be considered non-statutory. Use these examples to illustrate how an apparently technical-sounding claim may still be ineligible if it is an intangible concept or information per se (see In re Ferguson; Digitech Image Technologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals per se and computer-readable media (CRM) guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A transitory, propagating signal (e.g., a signal with embedded supplemental data) is not within one of the four statutory categories (In re Nuijten). Under BRI, computer readable media (CRM) will cover an ineligible signal per se unless the specification as filed provides a special definition distinguishing storage media from transmission media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification is silent, a claim to CRM or CRSM is ineligible unless amended to avoid the ineligible signal embodiment. It is acceptable to amend claims to exclude the signal embodiment by adding 'non-transitory' to modify the computer readable media ("non-transitory" is an option, not a requirement). It is not acceptable to merely add 'physical' or 'tangible' (Nuijten's ineligible signals were physical and tangible) nor acceptable to add 'storage' absent support in the original disclosure because BRI of CRSM commonly covers signals/carrier waves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Living subject matter and human organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonnaturally occurring non-human multicellular living organisms, including animals, may be eligible (see MPEP 2105 and 2014 Guidance). Claims directed to or encompassing a human organism are ineligible (Section 33(a) of the America Invents Act; 35 U.S.C. §101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the eligibility distinction between non-natural non-human organisms and human organisms; apply the statutory and AIA references when a claim potentially reads on a human organism. Use Form ¶ 7.04.03 for human-organism rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Useful' — the invention must have a specific, substantial, and credible utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the utility requirement under §101; see MPEP 2107 for Utility Guidelines. Ensure that claimed subject matter satisfies utility requirements as part of §101 considerations where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Whoever invents or discovers' — a patent may only be obtained by the person who engages in the act of inventing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications must include the name of the inventor for any invention claimed (35 U.S.C. 115(a)). Incorrect inventorship should be addressed using the appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., ¶ 7.04.101.aia or ¶ 7.04.102.aia) with explanatory text indicating why inventorship is incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections and appropriate form paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim under BRI covers non-statutory subject matter, the examiner must make a §101 rejection and use the appropriate form paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form ¶ 7.04.01 (reciting the statutory text), Form ¶ 7.05 ("Claim *** rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because …"), and Form ¶ 7.05.01 ("the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter because ***."). For human organisms use Form ¶ 7.04.03. For incorrect inventorship use Form ¶ 7.04.101.aia or 7.04.102.aia. Include explanatory specifics in the record for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of the record — examiner documentation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarifying the record benefits the Examiner, the Applicant, and the Public, places the Applicant on notice regarding the Office's position, and provides insight into the BRI for claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of clarifying actions: explain why the claim does not fit within one of the four categories (see MPEP 2106(I)), illustrate why the BRI of the claim encompasses a non-statutory embodiment (e.g., a signal per se), explain why the claim is interpreted to read on a human organism, and when the category is unclear add comments explaining the BRI. Clear recordation enables a more effective Applicant response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case law in eligibility determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply teachings from the full body of relevant case law (notably Alice, Myriad, Mayo, Bilski, In re Nuijten, In re Ferguson, Digitech) when conducting subject-matter eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2014 Interim Guidance reflects Supreme Court and Federal Circuit developments; examiners should consider these precedents in determining whether claims are directed to judicial exceptions or include additional elements amounting to significantly more. Cite relevant cases to support eligibility findings or rejections.
